title: Durlabhavardhana Claims the Naga Name
subtitle: How a Serpent Name Made a Mountain Kingdom into an Empire
region: Kashmir Valley, Srinagar region and the northwestern Himalaya
moral: Power lasts longer when it builds legitimacy, not fear.

sources.citation: Kalhana, Rajatarangini, Book III, vv. 475-514; trans. M.A. Stein, Kalhana's Rajatarangini, Vol. 1 (1900), pp. 86-95
sources.note: Main narrative for the founding; written about five centuries later and shaped by dynastic memory.

sources.citation: Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyouji, Kasmira chapter; trans. Samuel Beal, Buddhist Records of the Western World, Vol. 1 (1884), pp. 147-160
sources.note: Independent 7th-century report of a prosperous Kashmir with many monasteries and temples.

sources.citation: Debased gold dinar of Durlabhavardhana, Kushan-Sharada type, British Museum; illustrated in Karkota dynasty numismatic catalogues
sources.note: Physical attestation of the early dynasty and its inherited coin style.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle hero wide amid misty Himalaya

dialogue.text: In early Kashmir, a man of uncertain birth took the throne and said, “I am of the Karkota serpent line.” How could one name turn a hidden valley into a lasting power?

panels.shot: broad aerial establishing shot over Kashmir valley

dialogue.text: Seventh-century Kashmir was a mountain bowl of rivers and rice fields, temples and monasteries. Xuanzang saw a rich land, crowded with Brahmans and monks living side by side.

panels.shot: slow push-in toward a mixed religious district

dialogue.text: On one bank, Vedic fires burned; on the other, the Dharma was taught. Kashmir’s kings walked between shrines of Śiva and Buddha, balancing devotion with rule.

panels.shot: interior court long shot hinting a succession crisis

dialogue.text: Kalhana’s chronicle tells of earlier rulers fading and a throne left uncertain. Names like Baladitya and a daughter Anangalekha appear, but the details blur across five centuries.

panels.shot: medium shot introducing Durlabhavardhana at court edge

dialogue.text: From this haze emerges Durlabhavardhana. Kalhana calls him a retainer who rose close to the royal house, yet his true origins remain shadowed, half-remembered by later pens.

panels.shot: slow push-in close-up on Durlabhavardhana’s face

dialogue.text: Some say he took the throne through marriage into the ruling line; some doubt the tale. What is clear is this: in a time of uncertainty, he stood where power could not ignore him.

panels.shot: ceremonial wide shot of coronation scene

dialogue.text: At some point around the middle of the seventh century, he became king. The exact year slips through Kalhana’s fingers, yet the memory of a new house beginning holds firm.

panels.shot: symbolic overhead shot of throne platform and serpent carving

dialogue.text: To rule a valley of shrines and clans, a mere man was not enough. Durlabhavardhana reached for an older power: the serpents, the Nāgas who in Kashmir’s tales lived beneath its lakes.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of king before a Naga shrine

dialogue.text: Kalhana says he claimed descent from Karkotaka, a serpent king of Kashmiri lore. With that act, he bound his new line to a mythic guardian of the land itself.

panels.shot: medium shot of proclamation-like moment in assembly

dialogue.speaker: durlabhavardhana
dialogue.text: From Karkotaka’s line I rise. As his heir, I guard this valley.

panels.shot: slow pan across banners and motifs bearing serpent designs

dialogue.text: Thus the Karkota name was born: a dynasty linked to a Nāga, wrapped in the valley’s sacred stories. It was more than ornament; it was a claim to belong to Kashmir’s very soil.

panels.shot: coin macro shot with over-the-shoulder view of king

dialogue.text: His name also traveled in metal. Debased gold coins, in an old Kushan style with Śāradā letters, bear Durlabhavardhana’s mark. They show a ruler inheriting forms, yet stamping them anew.

panels.shot: wide shot of royal procession passing both temple and monastery

dialogue.text: Xuanzang, visiting Kashmir around this time, saw royal support flowing to monasteries and temples alike. A stable court allowed both to grow, even if the chronicler’s names differ.

panels.shot: intimate interior shot of king consulting Brahman and monk

dialogue.text: Kalhana remembers him, and later Karkotas, as patrons of learning and ritual. The details might shift, but the pattern holds: rulers drawing strength from many sacred tongues.

panels.shot: time-lapse style wide shot of palace over changing seasons

dialogue.text: Over decades, the Karkota house settled in. Whether Durlabhavardhana or his descendant Durlabhaka Pratapaditya was the stronger architect, the dynasty’s roots deepened in Kashmir’s ground.

panels.shot: historical montage of later Karkota might with ghosted founder image

dialogue.text: From this beginning came two centuries of Karkota rule, reaching beyond the valley. The serpent name, once a bold claim, became a banner under which kings expanded and endowed.

panels.shot: quiet close-up of older Durlabhavardhana by river at dusk

dialogue.text: We cannot know his private doubts—whether he still felt a retainer or truly a serpent king’s heir. History keeps his figure, yet leaves his inner voice as silent as the river.

panels.shot: final aerial shot over valley with faint serpent motif in terrain

dialogue.text: Durlabhavardhana’s power passed, but his choice endured: to anchor a new line in the valley’s own myths and faiths. In Kashmir’s history, his Karkota name shows that rule lasts longest when it grows from shared belief.
